selected.title: A Garden Is a Small Climate Conversation
selected.alt: A small balcony garden of succulents and green plants in natural light.
selected.caption: A garden can be a small climate conversation, lived one plant at a time.
selected.desc: A garden does not have to be large to change the way we look at the world. A few pots on a balcony can teach us about heat, water, soil and patience.

selected.title: In Praise of Small Joys
selected.alt: A child gently holding a duckling, forehead to forehead.
selected.caption: A child gently holding a duckling, forehead to forehead.
selected.desc: A child I know cupped a duckling in his hands last week and pressed his forehead to its head. I have not stopped thinking about his face.

selected.title: What Blue and Blaze Have Taught Me About Time
selected.alt: Blue and Blaze eating from their bowls in a photograph displayed on a laptop screen.
selected.caption: Blue and Blaze eating from their bowls in a photograph displayed on a laptop screen.
selected.desc: I used to think time belonged to the calendar. Now I think it belongs to whoever is waiting by the kitchen door.

library.title: When Love for One Dog Becomes Care for Many
library.alt: A rescue dog resting close to a person who is gently holding its face.
library.caption: Love for one dog can open the heart to many.
library.desc: Blue is my rescue Rottweiler. Loving him has quietly dismantled any idea I once held that rescue work is abstract or distant. You meet the dog in front of you first, the eyes that still carry old caution, the small daily tests of trust, the way a body learns it is finally safe. Only later do you feel the weight of all the others still waiting.

library.title: What Blue and Blaze Have Taught Me About Time
library.alt: Blue and Blaze eating from their bowls in a photograph displayed on a laptop screen.
library.caption: Blue and Blaze eating from their bowls in a photograph displayed on a laptop screen.
library.desc: I used to believe time belonged to the calendar. Now I think it belongs to whoever is waiting by the kitchen door.

library.title: Eco-Tips for Everyday Living
library.alt: A simple recycling guide held in a bright room.
library.caption: A practical guide to the materials we use and discard every day.
library.desc: Sustainability is not a lifestyle brand. It is a collection of small, sometimes inconvenient choices that somehow add up to a life you can stand behind. You do not need a bamboo toothbrush to begin. You only need a little curiosity and the willingness to ask why you do things the way you do.

library.title: A Garden Is a Small Climate Conversation
library.alt: A small balcony garden of succulents and green plants in natural light.
library.caption: A garden can be a small climate conversation, lived one plant at a time.
library.desc: A garden does not have to be large to change the way we look at the world. A few pots on a balcony can teach us about heat, water, soil and patience.

library.title: In Praise of Small Joys
library.alt: A child gently holding a duckling, forehead to forehead.
library.caption: A child gently holding a duckling, forehead to forehead.
library.desc: A child I know cupped a duckling in his hands last week and pressed his forehead to its head. I have not stopped thinking about his face.

library.title: Oceans in Focus: A Visual Essay
library.alt: A sea turtle gliding through vivid blue ocean waters, embodying marine grace.
library.caption: A sea turtle gliding through vivid blue ocean waters, embodying marine grace.
library.desc: The ocean does not care about our schedules. It moves to tides that were set in motion before the first human drew breath. That is what makes it humbling. Also terrifying, if I am honest. And that is what makes it necessary.

library.title: Rescue Stories That Restore Hope
library.alt: A volunteer gently supports a rescue dog.
library.caption: A volunteer gently supporting a rescue dog.
library.desc: There is a moment in every rescue story when fear turns to trust. It is not dramatic. It is quiet, so quiet you might miss it if you are not paying attention. A dog that flinched at every footstep begins to lean into a hand. A pigeon with a broken wing stops trying to fly away and simply breathes. These moments are the architecture of hope.

library.title: From Shelter to Sanctuary: One Dog’s Journey
library.alt: A black-and-white rescue dog standing in a bright shelter yard.
library.caption: A rescue dog standing in a bright shelter yard.
library.desc: The shelter smelled of disinfectant and hope. That is the only way I have found to describe it, though I have tried others. I met Blue on a Tuesday afternoon when the light was slanting through the high windows in gold bars. He was a Rottweiler puppy with paws too big for his body and eyes that held a gravity that stopped me.

library.title: What Trees Give Us Before We Notice
library.alt: Sunlight filtering through the leaves of a large green tree.
library.caption: Sunlight filtering through the leaves of a large green tree.
library.desc: There are trees I know by the way they change the light. I walk past them without always looking up, but I notice when one has been cut down. The pavement feels hotter. The street sounds harder. Something has disappeared before I have found the words for it.

library.title: Sustainable Living When the Forecast Is a Warning
library.alt: A houseplant being cared for at home.
library.caption: A houseplant being cared for at home, one small choice at a time.
library.desc: I used to think sustainable living was mostly a private discipline, the bin sorted properly, the water used carefully, a way of being tidy with the planet the way you might be tidy with a kitchen. Now I think it has to answer to something larger than tidiness, because the forecast has started making that unavoidable.

library.title: A Softer Monday
library.alt: A white alarm clock above a sign reading MONDAY on a bright blue background.
library.caption: A white alarm clock above a sign reading MONDAY on a bright blue background.
library.desc: Monday gets a bad name it does not fully deserve.

library.title: Affirmations, Self-Belief and the Stories We Repeat
library.alt: Colourful letters on a pink background spelling “You make a choice”.
library.caption: Colourful letters on a pink background spelling “You make a choice”.
library.desc: Affirmations are just you saying stuff to yourself on purpose. “I am enough.” “I can handle this.” “I’m getting better.” That is it.

library.title: Confidence After 40: A Quiet Revolution
library.alt: At ease in one's own body.
library.caption: At ease in one's own body.
library.desc: There is a particular confidence that arrives after forty. It does not announce itself with trumpets. (I wish it did. I would have noticed sooner.) It slips in through the back door, wearing comfortable shoes and sits down without asking permission.

library.title: The Discipline of Noticing Small Joys
library.alt: Clear quartz cradled in open hands.
library.caption: Clear quartz cradled in open hands.
library.desc: We are trained to notice what is wrong. The missed deadline. The slight insult. That one body part that refuses to behave. This negativity bias served our ancestors well. It kept them alive. But in a world where survival is less urgent, the same bias keeps us miserable.

library.title: Journaling Prompts for Stillness
library.alt: A figure turned toward its own reflection.
library.caption: A figure turned toward its own reflection.
library.desc: A journal is not a diary. It is not a record of what happened. It is a laboratory for what might happen if you thought differently. The page is the safest place I know.

library.title: Learning to Fail Without Becoming Smaller
library.alt: A Scrabble arrangement spelling FAILURE on a wooden table.
library.caption: Failure is part of learning. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: I used to think failure had a sound. It was the silence after an email went unanswered. The pause in a room when I had said too much. The small internal collapse that arrived when a plan I had believed in did not work, even though I had given it my best attention.

library.title: Three-Minute Morning Meditations
library.alt: A person meditating beside the water at sunrise.
library.caption: Three quiet minutes can change the shape of a morning. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: You do not need an hour. You do not need a cushion. You do not need to chant in Sanskrit or burn incense. You need three minutes. A chair. And the willingness to stop.

library.title: The Day the Light Stepped Aside
library.alt: A partial eclipse glowing through pale clouds.
library.caption: Sometimes light returns in an unexpected shape. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: The eclipse is not here. It is in Spain. Today the moon crosses the sun over southern Europe and half the world is travelling to stand beneath it. I am not. I am reading about it from here, the way you read about a wedding you were not invited to but are glad is happening.

library.title: The Life You Keep Beginning
library.alt: A runner poised at a starting line on a track.
library.caption: There is more than one way to begin again. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: There have been several beginnings in my life. Some were planned. Some arrived because the old way could not continue. I used to think beginning again meant I had failed to settle. Now I think it can mean that I am still listening.

library.title: The Path Less Travelled
library.alt: A winding road through a green mountain landscape, seen from above.
library.caption: The road does not need to be straight to be yours. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: Everyone told me to take the safe road. I did not always listen.

library.title: The Voice You Use With Yourself
library.alt: A woman writing in a notebook in soft natural light.
library.caption: A woman writing in a notebook in soft natural light.
library.desc: I used to think confidence meant speaking loudly enough that nobody could misunderstand me. I know better now. Some of the strongest changes in my life began quietly, with the way I spoke to myself when nobody else could hear.

library.title: What Mentoring Has Taught Me About Advice
library.alt: Two people holding warm drinks across a table during a conversation.
library.caption: Good advice often begins by making room for another person’s question. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: Two cups of tea sit on a small table between two chairs. One steam ring has already cooled to a pale bloom on the saucer. We have both been here before, not always with the same names, not always the same questions, but the same human tendency to want a tidy answer handed across the table.

library.title: Abstract Tech: Visual Language of the Future
library.alt: Abstract neon tech patterns creating a futuristic visual language.
library.caption: Abstract neon tech patterns creating a futuristic visual language.
library.desc: Technology has developed its own aesthetic. Neon grids. Glitch effects. Holographic interfaces. These visuals are not just decoration. They are a visual language that signals innovation, futurity and the dissolution of boundaries between physical and digital.

library.title: AI as a Creative Companion
library.alt: A bright creative workspace with a leafy plant, camera, monitor and soft afternoon light.
library.caption: A bright creative workspace where ideas can take shape alongside technology.
library.desc: I think technology should feel like an extension of what you actually want to do, not a replacement for thinking. The best tools are the ones that get out of your way and let you think more clearly, create more freely and connect more deeply.

library.title: When Technology Has to Explain Itself
library.alt: A woman reading a book about what technology should explain.
library.caption: A woman reads about the questions technology asks of us. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: I read something this morning that made me put my cup down.

library.title: The Rise of Digital Rituals
library.alt: Phone and laptop arranged in a clean digital workspace.
library.caption: Phone and laptop arranged in a clean digital workspace.
library.desc: We think of rituals as ancient. Candles. Chants. Offerings. But the human need for ritual is not bound to any technology. It is bound to intention.

library.title: The Future Should Still Have Room for People
library.alt: People working together around a table with laptops and notes.
library.caption: People working together around a table with laptops and notes.
library.desc: I am interested in technology when it brings people into better conversations, not when it tries to make the people unnecessary. A tool can organise a meeting, find a pattern, or help with a first draft. It cannot decide what matters to the people sitting around the table.

library.title: What Responsible AI Means on an Ordinary Day
library.alt: A close view of a person using technology while considering its human impact.
library.caption: Technology matters most when we ask what it means for real people.
library.desc: I have spent the past year working closely with AI tools and I am interested in what they mean beyond the excitement. The important questions are often ordinary ones. What happens to our privacy? Who is responsible when an answer is wrong? Does a useful tool give us time back, or does it quietly take over our judgement?

library.title: Building a Second Brain
library.alt: Creative coding and digital design workspace with multiple screens.
library.caption: Creative coding and digital design workspace with multiple screens.
library.desc: Your mind is for having ideas, not holding them. That is the idea behind the second brain movement and honestly, it has changed how I think. Externalise your thinking so that your biological brain is free to do what it does best: connect, create and wonder.

library.title: The Difference Between Assistance and Dependence
library.alt: People absorbed in their phones, illustrating the line between digital assistance and dependence.
library.caption: People absorbed in their phones, illustrating the line between digital assistance and dependence. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: My favourite mornings begin with the tactile ritual of shutting my laptop, nudging a notebook towards me and making a single neat line down the margin. The gesture is small and domestic. It is also a test. Closing the laptop does not make the world less clever. What it does is remind me that some decisions need human attention, the sort of attention that cannot be outsourced to the pleasing certainty of a search result or an algorithmic nudge.

library.title: What AI Can Give Back to a Human Day
library.alt: A laptop, tea and handwritten notes in a calm working space.
library.caption: A laptop, tea and handwritten notes in a calm working space. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: On the kitchen table this morning my laptop sat beside a sheaf of handwritten notes and a cooling cup of tea. The notes were flecked with scribbles and arrows and the kind of small, useful mistakes that tell you you have been thinking for yourself. The laptop offered a different kind of promise, pages of text waiting to be nudged into shape. I have been learning how to let the two coexist rather than compete. The question I keep returning to is not what AI can do for me but what it can give back to the human parts of my day.

library.title: A Day Without Eating
library.alt: A bright plate arranged with a clock, fork and knife, representing time, food and fasting.
library.caption: A bright plate arranged with a clock, fork and knife, representing time, food and fasting.
library.desc: I used to think fasting was a discipline you performed for someone else to notice. A neat achievement, mentioned once it was safely over.

library.title: Fifth Place and Fine With It
library.alt: Fifth place on the board, names of others kept private.
library.caption: Fifth place on the board, names of others kept private.
library.desc: I used to think a step count was just a number competing with other numbers. Now I think it might be one of the more honest measures of a life I have.

library.title: Inside the Sauna
library.alt: The still heat of a wooden sauna.
library.caption: The still heat of a wooden sauna.
library.desc: The sauna is a small wooden room that smells of cedar and effort. I've been using it for two years now and I still feel a small thrill every time I open the door. Like I'm about to step into somewhere that demands my full attention.

library.title: Movement as Medicine
library.alt: A woman stretching in the morning light.
library.caption: A woman stretching in the morning light.
library.desc: The body isn't a machine. It's a landscape. Weather and seasons and terrain that shifts whether you ask it to or not. It has weather and seasons and terrain that changes with use and disuse. Movement is how we tend that landscape.

library.title: What a Nervous System Reset Really Means
library.alt: A man standing beside a window with his hand resting against his face.
library.caption: A man standing beside a window with his hand resting against his face.
library.desc: Your nervous system is basically the body’s alarm and recovery system. It’s constantly scanning for threat or safety. When life piles on deadlines, notifications, arguments, traffic, old stress that never fully left it can get stuck in “on” mode. Heart rate up, muscles tight, mind racing, gut unsettled. That’s the sympathetic side running the show (fight, flight, or freeze).

library.title: Conversations with a Reiki Practitioner
library.alt: Hands held just above the body in a reiki session.
library.caption: Hands held just above the body in a reiki session.
library.desc: I met Amara at a wellness fair in Johannesburg. Her table was modest. A few crystals. A business card. A calm that seemed to radiate from her skin. I was sceptical. I am still sceptical. But I was also curious.

library.title: Rest Is Not a Reward
library.alt: A wicker basket of books, dried flowers, fruit and folded textiles in warm natural light.
library.caption: A wicker basket of books, dried flowers, fruit and folded textiles in warm natural light.
library.desc: I have treated rest as something I could earn for a long time. Finish the work. Answer the messages. Be useful. Then perhaps there would be a quiet afternoon waiting for me at the end of it all.

library.title: The Body Is Not a Project
library.alt: A woman moving on a treadmill in a bright gym.
library.caption: A woman moving on a treadmill in a bright gym.
library.desc: There are days when movement feels joyful and days when it feels like one more demand. I have learned that both can be true without turning the body into a problem to solve.

library.title: The Quiet Work of Continuing
library.alt: A woman reading a book outdoors beside a quiet stretch of water.
library.caption: A quiet moment of reading outdoors. Photograph via Pexels, cottonbro studio.
library.desc: There is a version of persistence that looks impressive from a distance. It has clean mornings, strong opinions and a calendar full of evidence that someone is moving forward.

library.title: The Run I Hadn't Trained For
library.alt: A runner's shoes on a treadmill during a five-kilometre challenge.
library.caption: The moment before the shins had their say.
library.desc: I used to think showing up was most of the job. If I turned up willing, I assumed the rest would sort itself out.

library.title: Do Wellness Trackers Really Work?
library.alt: A black Oura ring standing on a soft grey textured surface.
library.caption: A black Oura ring standing on a soft grey textured surface.
library.desc: I strapped an Oura Ring to my finger and a Garmin to my wrist and waited for enlightenment. Spoiler: it didn't arrive in a push notification. The devices promised data. Sleep stages. Heart rate variability. Recovery scores. After three months, I had to ask: did I feel any better?

library.title: What GLP-1 Actually Means and What My Own Sugar Habit Taught Me
library.alt: An abstract image of a syringe above an apple.
library.caption: An abstract image of a syringe above an apple.
library.desc: I used to hear GLP-1 mentioned as though it were a brand rather than a hormone, another word in the general noise around weight loss drugs. I want to explain it properly, because I think most people repeating the term have never actually been told what it means.

library.title: What My Oura Ring Taught Me About Sleep
library.alt: A woman sleeping beside a smartphone in soft morning light.
library.caption: A woman sleeping beside a smartphone in soft morning light.
library.desc: There is a small circle of metal I take off the moment I wash my hands and rest on the bedside table beside whatever book I am reading. It is unobtrusive in a way a wristband is not. It feels private and a little companionable. Wearing it has not turned me into a perfect sleeper. What it has done is change how I notice sleep and how quickly I equate a number with either success or failure.

library.title: A World Made Smaller by Birds
library.alt: A person walking through dense green forest beside tall ferns.
library.caption: A small walk can make a much larger world feel close.
library.desc: I was making a cup of tea the other morning when a flash of white and black cut across the grey sky and for a few minutes the garden felt as if it were linked by invisible thread to somewhere far beyond the rooftops. Birds have that effect, drawing distant places into the small patch of earth we can see from our windows.

library.title: Conservation Begins with Attention
library.alt: A hand writing in a notebook beside a warm drink.
library.caption: Care often begins with the simple act of paying attention.
library.desc: There is something modest and stubborn about attention. It does not demand grand gestures or specialist knowledge. It is the act of turning your head, slowing your pace and noticing what is already happening around you.

library.title: Rainforest After Rain
library.alt: A sea turtle gliding through clear blue water.
library.caption: A living landscape carries stories of weather, water and time.
library.desc: There is something about the moment right after the rain stops that always makes me slow down, the way the air changes and the forest seems to have a new patience. I find myself listening before I look, because the sounds tell you more than the shapes.

library.title: The Air We Share
library.alt: A vivid, plant-lined street in Cape Town.
library.caption: The air around us is shared, even when our lives feel separate.
library.desc: I often notice the air before I see anything else. On some mornings it comes cool and sharp, carrying the faint yeast of a baker’s van and the metallic tang of the river. On others it is heavy with the soft, sweet smoke of a neighbour’s wood burner and the dust of last night’s traffic. It feels intimate in a way that birdsong does not, because it moves through the rooms where we live and reaches into the lungs of the smallest and oldest among us.

library.title: What We Owe the Soil
library.alt: Hands tending a leafy houseplant in a sunlit room.
library.caption: Care for the soil begins with noticing what keeps life going.
library.desc: I think about soil more often than most might expect. There is a certain humility in watching a handful of earth crumble between your fingers and recognising that most of what supports us is quiet, dark and underfoot. It keeps growing things alive, stores water, holds stories of seasons and footsteps and does all this without noise or credit.

library.title: A Tool Is Only as Wise as the Question
library.alt: A hand writes in a notebook beside a laptop.
library.caption: A hand writes in a notebook beside a laptop. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: There is something almost ritual about setting a cup of tea down and looking out at the small rectangle of sky my kitchen window offers. It is an ordinary pause, but it reminds me that tools are best judged by the company they keep. A perfectly good kettle will not warm a cold room and a clever app will not find the answer you need unless you know how to ask it. The way we frame a question sets the direction of everything that follows.

library.title: Can AI Help the Climate Without Becoming Another Cost?
library.alt: People wading through a flooded street, showing the human stakes of climate change.
library.caption: People wade through a flooded street, showing the human stakes of climate change. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: Lately I have been thinking about the neat, clever tools that promise to help us meet climate goals. They can do startling things with data, spot patterns we would otherwise miss and suggest where resources might be stretched further. But as useful as these systems can be, I worry we too easily treat them as a simple fix, rather than as something that needs careful tending.

library.title: Can Technology Help Us Notice More?
library.alt: A phone photographs a landscape, showing technology helping us look more closely.
library.caption: A phone photographs a landscape, showing technology helping us look more closely. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: I have a small ritual of standing at the kitchen sink for a minute before I turn on the kettle, partly because it feels like an odd kind of permission to just be. Lately I have been aware of how much the tools in my pocket and on my wrist shape that minute and whether they help me notice the things I want to notice.

library.title: The Cost of Convenience
library.alt: People with a shopping trolley and a message about the cost of convenience.
library.caption: People stand with a shopping trolley and a message about the cost of convenience. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: I make a cup of tea, the kettle humming on its own and a notification tells me my shopping will arrive in an hour. There is a small comfort in that certainty. It means no trolley-wrangling in the rain, no rummaging for loose change at the shop counter and no need to plan the day around opening hours. It also nudges a question that sits quietly at the back of my mind: at what point does ease start to cost more than money?

library.title: When a Recommendation Becomes a Narrowing
library.alt: A person uses a phone showing a music recommendation list.
library.caption: A person uses a phone showing a music recommendation list. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: There is a peculiar economy to suggestions. One small nudge on my screen and the afternoon seems to rearrange itself, as if the app, the playlist or the online shop has quietly decided what I ought to like next.

library.title: The Infrastructure We Forget
library.alt: Rows of servers in a data centre, showing the physical infrastructure behind digital life.
library.caption: Rows of servers in a data centre, showing the physical infrastructure behind digital life. Photograph via Pexels.
library.desc: I was making a pot of tea the other morning and noticed the kettle click off before I had time to breathe. It felt like a small miracle, which of course it is when you think about the wire and metal and company of engineers that make that single familiar sound possible.

library.title: A Letter to the Woman Still Becoming
library.alt: A handwritten letter held beside a rose in warm natural light.
library.caption: A handwritten letter held beside a rose in warm natural light.
library.desc: I am writing because some afternoons the house is quiet enough for thoughts to land and stay and a quiet kindness feels overdue.

library.title: How to Stay Tender Without Becoming Naive
library.alt: A woman sitting beside a bright window with flowering plants.
library.caption: Tenderness can be a way of seeing clearly, not a refusal to know better.
library.desc: There is a softness I keep like a favourite mug, easy to reach for and, if I am honest, sometimes at risk of being chipped.

library.title: Learning to Take Up Space Kindly
library.alt: An older woman smiling with a bright bouquet against a sunny background.
library.caption: Taking up space can be generous when it makes room for others too.
library.desc: There is a strange, familiar tug when someone else fills the room with their laugh, their volume, their presence and you find yourself literally shrinking.

library.title: The Courage to Be Seen Learning
library.alt: A hand writing music on a chalkboard during practice.
library.caption: A hand writing music on a chalkboard during practice.
library.desc: Sitting with a warm cup of tea, I often find my thoughts returning to the same awkward, delightful problem.

library.title: The Difference Between Company and Connection
library.alt: Two women sharing a conversation among green plants.
library.caption: Company fills a room. Connection changes how we leave it.
library.desc: There are times when a room full of people feels like background noise and a single conversation feels like an anchor.

library.title: What I Learnt from Travelling Alone
library.alt: A blue-flowering path leading through a green landscape.
library.caption: Travelling alone teaches the ear to hear its own questions.
library.desc: There is a peculiar kind of quiet the moment you button your coat and walk out by yourself, suitcase in hand.

library.title: The Small Rituals That Make a Day Softer
library.alt: Two people surrounded by vivid pink flowers in a bright garden.
library.caption: Small joys are not distractions from life. They are part of its structure.
library.desc: There is a particular comfort in doing something small and ordinary on purpose.

library.title: When the Old Version of You Calls
library.alt: A dancer seen from behind with one arm raised, suggesting movement and an emerging self.
library.caption: A dancer seen from behind with one arm raised, suggesting movement and an emerging self.
library.desc: Sometimes, late in the evening when the washing-up has been done and there is a mug of tea cooling at my elbow, I hear the old version of me on the line.

library.title: Ageing Without Apology
library.alt: A person cycling along a quiet tree-lined road in soft daylight.
library.caption: Ageing is not an apology. It is a life continuing to become more itself.
library.desc: There is a small, steady pleasure in noticing how my days have shifted shape.

library.title: The Health Advice I No Longer Chase
library.alt: A fresh plate of greens and vegetables on a pale table.
library.caption: Health advice is useful only when it leaves room for a real human life.
library.desc: Health advice arrives daily, bright and certain, offering a neat formula for looking, feeling or performing better.

library.title: The Medicine of a Good Laugh
library.alt: A warm cup of tea catching the light beside a dark tabletop.
library.caption: A good laugh can change the temperature of an ordinary day.
library.desc: You know that little alchemy that happens when a laugh breaks out?

library.title: The Wellness Event as a Shared Room
library.alt: A person sitting in a quiet room beside a window.
library.caption: A shared room can give wellbeing a little more room to breathe.
library.desc: I turned up to a local wellness event the way you might arrive at someone's flat for an evening.

library.title: Thriving Is More Than Feeling Fine
library.alt: A bright, plant-filled room with a sauna and soft pink textiles.
library.caption: Thriving has a warmer, messier edge than simply feeling fine.
library.desc: I often think of thriving as a slightly more honest word than happiness.

library.title: What My Garmin Taught Me About Effort
library.alt: A pair of green running shoes ready for a five-kilometre challenge.
library.caption: A pair of green running shoes ready for a five-kilometre challenge.
library.desc: When I first strapped a Garmin to my wrist I expected it to be a strict accountant of exertion.

library.title: What the Body Knows Before the App Does
library.alt: A black health-tracking ring resting on a pale surface.
library.caption: A black health-tracking ring resting on a pale surface.
library.desc: There is a small, steady voice that lives in the margins of my day. It is not loud, it does not arrive with a notification sound.
